EU warned that strikes by "Iran’s proxies" risk pushing the region into a wider cycle of violence. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the attack as a “dangerous escalation” and called on the Houthis to stop targeting civilian infrastructure. “These attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwaves sent through the world. These murderous attacks on civilians must stop at once,” the EU chief wrote on X on Sunday. She added that the EU stood in “solidarity with Saudi Arabia”. items.summary: Houthis claim responsibility for deadly Riyadh airport attack Yemen’s Houthis say they carried out Saturday’s missile attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid Airport, which killed 12 people and wounded about 300, some critically. Military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched several operations against the airport, “resulting in the disruption of air traffic at the airport and its complete closure”. He also named King Fahd Airport in Dammam, an Aramco-affiliated petrol station and a refinery in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Region as targets. The Riyadh strike caused the highest death toll from an attack on a Gulf country since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on 28 February. King Khalid Airport remained closed on Sunday.

"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. "We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd.” Trump’s statement came after several news sites, including Axios, which is seen as close to Trump and his aides, reported that the Pentagon was preparing for a resumption of high-intensity strikes on Iran. items.title: Why Saudi Arabia has returned to war in Yemen
items.summary: This article was republished with permission from the Arab Center Washington DC. When Ansar Allah—commonly referred to as the Houthis— seized Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandab Strait on September 10, 2026, they appeared to gain the upper hand in Yemen’s long-running conflict. However, in early October Saudi-backed government forces began to retake some of the captured territory and Saudi Arabia launched a punishing assault on Houthi positions from the air. France , Pakistan , and the United States have all sent personnel to help the kingdom counter the Houthi offensive. Outside the region, some have portrayed the Houthi offensive as another theater within the broader US-Israeli war on Iran. However, this broader regional war is separate from the war in Yemen, which can be traced back to the Houthi takeover of Yemen’s capital Sanaa in September 2014 and the decision by neighboring Saudi Arabia to launch a coalition to oust them in March 2015. items.summary: Trump says he does not believe China and Russia help Iran, contradicting US intelligence President Donald Trump said on Monday he did not believe that China and Russia were helping Iran "at all", even as US intelligence reports in recent months have found that both countries directly support Tehran. Trump said on Truth Social that he had seen comments from his critics and opponents that China and Russia were helping Iran. Moscow and Beijing maintain close ties with Tehran. "If they are, it's at a very low level, but I don't believe they are at all. They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast," Trump wrote. US intelligence assessments from recent months have shown that Russia and China are providing military support to Iran in the form of satellite imagery for targeting purposes and components for weapons, according to two people briefed on the matter.

items.title: Two Indian nationals missing after drone attack on tanker off Oman's coast
items.summary: Two Indian nationals missing after drone attack on tanker off Oman's coast A drone attack on a vessel off the coast of Oman left two Indian nations missing, a senior Indian official said on Sunday. Meanwhile, nine others were rescued, as search and rescue operations by the local coast guard begin. "On Oct 11, tanker MT PETRO DOLPHIN, carrying 11 Indian seafarers, was subjected to a drone attack at Sohar Anchorage," Indian Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said in a post on X. "While nine of our Indian crew members have been successfully rescued and are safe, two Indian nationals currently remain missing." Sonowal added that India is "continuously coordinating with all relevant authorities to fully support the ongoing rescue efforts and ensure every possible action is taken to safely locate our missing personnel". Since the war on Iran began in late February, at least 16 Indian seafarers have been killed.

items.title: 'Going bankrupt': Iran shopkeepers struggle as war dims demand
items.summary:
Iran's economy has been battered by years of sanctions, but the conflict that began in February with US-Israeli attacks and an American blockade of the country's ports has put extra strain on daily life.
 
Rising inflation, nearly 90 percent year-on-year in September according to official figures, and erratic currency exchange fluctuations have driven up the cost of everyday items. Food prices have more than doubled since last year.

clusters.headline: Pakistan president urges Iran, US to honour Islamabad MoU

items.title: Pakistan president urges Iran, US to honour Islamabad MoU
items.summary: Pakistan president urges Iran, US to honour Islamabad MoU Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari has urged the US and Iran to exercise restraint and honour their commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding. The MoU is a 14-point interim peace agreement signed electronically on 17-18 June between the United States and Iran, with Pakistan acting as the primary mediator. Zardari called for differences to be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, emphasising the importance of safe maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, according to a statement from his office. His remarks came during a meeting with Russian Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev in Islamabad. Zardari warned that the conflict posed serious challenges to regional stability, global energy security, trade and supply chains, stressing the need to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states. Kolokoltsev is on a four-day official visit to Pakistan, the first by a Russian interior minister to the South Asian country.

clusters.headline: Attacks on Hormuz shipping at wartime high, report says

items.title: Attacks on Hormuz shipping at wartime high, report says
items.summary: Attacks on Hormuz shipping at wartime high, report says Iranian missile and drone attacks on ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz were at their most intense in the two weeks to 11 October, the highest level since the US-Israeli strikes began seven months ago, the Financial Times reported. The next most intense period of attacks was during the first two weeks of March, when 13 ships were hit, the newspaper said, citing data from naval agency UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which monitors marine security in the region. Shipowners are reconsider carrying cargoes in the region, the report said. Six vessels were attacked on Sunday alone, making it the deadliest day of attacks on shipping near the strait since the start of the conflict, FT calculated. It added that oil shipments through Hormuz fell to just 2.9 million barrels on 11 October, the lowest daily volume this month, according to Kpler.

At the time of writing, the missile strike on King Khalid international airport has killed at least 13 people and left 300 injured, marking a significant turn in a regional conflagration that is only getting more intense. It was the single most deadly attack on any Gulf country since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February. In Saudi Arabia, a country that is unaccustomed to such fatalities, the death toll is bewilderingly high and likely to prompt a bloody response. Over the past year, the Gulf has entered a new era of instability that is not temporary and cannot be reversed. Toch kwam er wat beeld van de aanval naar buiten: VN-gezant voor Jemen Hans Grundberg noemt de aanval een ernstige escalatie. clusters.headline: Iran’s security chief accuses Trump administration of oil smuggling near Oman

items.title: Iran’s security chief accuses Trump administration of oil smuggling near Oman
items.summary: Iran’s security chief accuses Trump administration of oil smuggling near Oman Mohsen Rezaei has accused the Trump administration of recruiting “thugs” to smuggle oil through coastal waters off Oman. Iran’s Supreme National Security Council secretary said the UAE military and the commander of US Central Command also participate in the operation, according to state-linked news agency ISNA. Trump “claims every day that the Strait of Hormuz is open, but in response I say: ‘You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iranian control and we manage it,'” Rezaei said. He said the operation relies on a handful of “small vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers”, adding that Iran attacks them “every night”.

items.title: Iran security chief accuses Trump of ‘smuggling’ oil through Hormuz
items.summary: Iran security chief accuses Trump of ‘smuggling’ oil through Hormuz Iran’s security chief claimed on Sunday that US President Donald Trump's adminitation hired “thugs” in the coastal waters of Oman to smuggle oil through the Iranian blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Trump “claims every day that the Strait of Hormuz is open, but in response I say: ‘You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iranian control and we manage it,'” Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei was quoted as saying by Iran's ISNA news agency. Rezaei said that the smuggling operation involves the UAE military and the commander of US Central Command (Centcom) using a handful of “small vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers” and that Iran targets them “every night”.

Tegen nieuwssite Al Jazeera zegt ze: "Ik denk nog steeds dat de Saudi's de-escalatie willen. Ze willen geen langdurige escalatie. Mogelijk is een eerste militaire reactie al begonnen. Houthi-milities melden een Saudische aanval op de door hen gecontroleerde luchthaven van Sanaa. items.title: Iranian nuclear technology safe from US attacks, says atomic energy chief
items.summary: Iranian nuclear technology safe from US attacks, says atomic energy chief The head of Iran's atomic energy agency said on Sunday that the country's nuclear technology is safe from external disruption and cannot be halted by threats, pressure or attacks. Mohammad Eslami, the chief of the Atomic Energy Organisation of Iran (AEOI), said Iran's nuclear advances are a national achievement and were a testament to the dedication of Iranian scientists. “Overt threats by US officials to use tactical weapons against Iran’s nuclear facilities - delivered right from the United Nations podium - and talk of destroying Iran’s ancient civilisation, reveal helplessness in the face of a pioneering nation that has historically been the cradle of science, knowledge and technology,” Eslami was quoted as saying by Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency, adding that the nation will not surrender to excessive demands. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly affirmed Washington's intention to wipe out Iran's nuclear capabilities and ensure that the country will never be able to develop the technology.

Asked why possible US military action against Iran might be delayed until after the 3 November midterm elections rather than carried out immediately, Trump told reporters: “Well, we may. I think we’ll see, but I think that, uh, they’re failing badly. Their country is failing badly." "The military is defeated. They have no navy, they have no air force. Uh, they have 300 percent inflation and, uh, Iran is in very bad shape.” The remarks, recorded in a transcript of Trump’s 9 October press briefing, did not include a specific timeline or details of what action Washington might take. items.summary: Israeli politician says assassinating Ali Khamenei was a ‘mistake’ The leader of Israel’s Democrats party on Saturday has called the assassination of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei a “mistake”. “I think, unequivocally, the elimination of Khamenei, the father, was a mistake - not because he didn’t deserve to die, only because it doesn’t serve the interests of the State of Israel,” Yair Golan said. He also added that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s goal of toppling the Iranian government was “unrealistic”. Khamenei was assassinated at the beginning of the US-Israel war and has been succeeded by his son, Mojtaba. The new supreme leader is believed to be far less risk-averse than his father, who had issued a fatwa in 2003 banning nuclear weapons in Iran. items.title: Increased vessel attacks drive Hormuz oil exports 'sharply lower', report says
items.summary: Increased vessel attacks drive Hormuz oil exports 'sharply lower', report says Hormuz oil exports were “sharply lower,” falling to a seven-day average of 9.9 million barrels per day as of October 7, 42 percent below prewar levels and down from about 15.5 million in September, according to Kpler data cited by the Financial Times. Kpler said that flows had recovered to prewar levels in September but "intensified attacks on vessels" had driven exports "sharply lower" this week. Energy analyst Rory Johnston also said that the latest estimate puts Hormuz seven-day average oil flow peaking at 16.2 mbpd on September 24. "Then Iran really picked up its shipping attacks and that flow unsurprisingly pulled back by 3-4 mbpd," he wrote on X. "Now seeing flow at 12-13 mbpd over the past two weeks."

clusters.headline: US leaves Iraq: 'Shock and awe' curdles into 'Aw, shucks'

items.title: US leaves Iraq: 'Shock and awe' curdles into 'Aw, shucks'
items.summary: The Bunker appears originally at the Project on Government Oversight and is republished here with permission. The U.S. ended its military campaign in Iraq on September 30, as the final American combat troops based there left the country. Their departure ended 23 years of fitful fighting. They found no weapons of mass destruction , which was the battering ram President George W. Bush and his combative coterie used to scaremonger the U.S to invade in 2003. The first time the window-rattling roar of a B-1 bomber woke me up this summer, I thought for one crazed second we were under attack. By the second time, I’d learned to recognise the sound of US planes taking off from their base at RAF Fairford for what it was: a reminder that although Britain wants no part in this war with Iran, we cannot quite escape the consequences. We’ll feel them at the petrol pump , or in the supermarket this autumn, or in this winter’s heating bills . But living under the flight path adds an extra edge to it. The skies finally fell silent last week, but only because the bombers have been hastily summoned home after an alleged terrorist plot to attack Fairford, in which (according to the prime minister) there are “ strong indications that Iran played a part ”. items.summary: In Noorwegen wordt morgen bekendgemaakt wie dit jaar de Nobelprijs voor de Vrede krijgt. Dat ligt hoogstwaarschijnlijk al vast, maar ongeacht wie de winnaar wordt, zal het wenkbrauwen doen fronsen in het Witte Huis. De Amerikaanse president zal de vredesprijs namelijk niet krijgen, is de verwachting. Vorig jaar riep president Trump zichzelf tot rechtmatige winnaar uit. De Nobelprijs werd echter uitgereikt aan de Venezolaanse oppositieleider María Corina Machado voor "haar onvermoeibare inzet voor het bevorderen van democratische rechten voor de bevolking van Venezuela". Het Witte Huis bekritiseerde het Nobelcomité omdat het "politiek boven vrede" zou hebben laten gaan. Trump beweerde dat hij "acht oorlogen" had beëindigd en dat daarom alleen hij de prijs verdiende. Later bood Machado haar prijs alsnog aan Trump aan tijdens een bezoek aan het Witte Huis, kort nadat de VS de Venezolaanse president Maduro had gevangengenomen. items.title: Is Iran poised to withdraw from the Non-Proliferation Treaty?
items.summary: In September, as the media focused its attention on the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz and the debates at the U.N. General Assembly, some internal developments in Iran went all but unnoticed. On September 28, 32 Iranian conservatives published an open letter calling for Iran to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) as a matter of urgency. Since the “ snapback ” of U.N. sanctions on Iran in September 2025, ultraconservative Iranian lawmakers have regularly pushed for pulling out of the NPT, under which the vast majority of states have committed to not develop nuclear weapons. The Majles — Iran’s parliament — drafted a law that would have initiated the move in 2025, but it has yet to move forward. In September, some lawmakers submitted new “triple-urgency” legislation to the Majles ’ president, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, who is also currently Iran’s chief negotiator These continuous calls by ultraconservatives to withdraw from the NPT have yet to produce an actual withdrawal because of a lack of political consensus. items.title: Will Americans ever escape this 'imperialist realism'?
items.summary: Last week, after nearly two decades of fighting, the U.S. finally pulled the plug on its seemingly endless war in Iraq. Like our exit from Afghanistan just a few years ago, the end of fighting in Iraq was met with an eerie quiet. It doesn’t take much to figure out why so little attention is paid to the end of these wars: they mark yet another loss for America and the people in Washington who insist our military power can solve every problem, everywhere. Both conflicts are examples of American hubris — strategically incoherent wars fought with American lives at the expense of too many Iraqis and Afghans lives. But, of course, we refuse to learn our lesson. The week before Americans finally vacated Iraq, President Donald Trump took to his proverbial pulpit at the U.N. to brag about his exploitation of Venezuela for oil, declaring “to the victor goes the spoils.” It was a stark expression of how America’s domination of the global order — it’s imperialism, if you will — really works. items.summary: The Geoeconomic Implications of the Iran War: An Early Examination Antoine Thu, 10/08/2026 - 02:00 Strategic Security Analyses Global Key points Globalisation has rested on a set of functions long treated as background conditions: transit through maritime choke points, insurability, dollar settlement, critical material inputs and protection by a hegemonic power. In practice, each is an excludable asset held by an identifiable actor, and the Iran war has demonstrated that they can be withheld and monetised. The war followed the failure of the most ambitious campaign of economic coercion yet attempted. In this campaign, sanctions functioned as an antechamber to military action rather than as its substitute, and the resort to a naval blockade to halt Iranian oil exports amounted to an admission that the financial coercion strategy had failed. Iran’s monetisation of the Strait of Hormuz followed a path already opened by US tariffs and export controls, and by Chinese restrictions on critical materials. items.title: The Guardian view on the US midterms: the cost of living is on the ballot, but this is about democracy too | Editorial
items.summary: Donald Trump’s unpopularity and the economic struggles of voters have boosted Democrats. But with less than a month to go, there is no complacency For once, Democrats and Donald Trump might be in agreement: “Pretend I’m on the ticket,” the historically unpopular president has instructed supporters . Midterms are in large part a referendum on the incumbent, and Trump’s war on Iran and its impact on the cost of living have boosted support for Democrats. With less than a month to go, they have reason to be upbeat . The party has a mountain to climb after the devastating defeats of 2024, and the gerrymandering of Republicans, but surveys give it a lead of about nine points on the generic ballot, which measures preference for parties rather than specific candidates. Attention has turned from the prospects of seizing the House, where Democrats are forecast a clear majority, to what once seemed like the highly optimistic possibility of taking the Senate too. While the world looks on in dismay at his farcical war in Iran, the thuggery of Ice agents or clownish attacks on erstwhile allies like Canada and Denmark, the core functions of the American government are slowly disintegrating. It is harder to get people to focus on the machinery of the state because the effects are often slow and hard to pin down. Outbreaks of disease – such as the recent wave of explosive diarrhoea across the US – might have happened anyway, but were probably made worse by lay-offs at the Centers for Disease Control. Likewise, Trump is not directly responsible for natural disasters, but response times in the past year may have been hampered by mass redundancies at the National Weather Service. items.title: US and several allies say Iran committed 'terrorist actions'
items.summary: US and several allies say Iran committed 'terrorist actions' The US and nine other countries across the Americas in a joint statement condemned what they called Iran's "terrorist actions". The joint statement was released by the US and endorsed by Argentina, Canada, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Guyana, Paraguay, Peru, and Trinidad and Tobago. "On 5 October, the undersigned nations, condemn the terrorist actions and other malign influence operations in our hemisphere by Iran and its terrorist proxies," it read. "These hostile efforts include a range of Iranian and proxy-sponsored lethal plotting, illicit fundraising, political interference and foreign influence activities, and operations meant to bolster terrorist networks, coerce perceived enemies, compromise legal or administrative processes, and harm regional security." The joint statement indicated that the countries "stand united" against "such threats", demanding that Tehran and "its proxies must halt these actions now".

clusters.headline: Saudi Aramco chief warns of 'scarily thin’ global oil stockpiles, amid war on Iran

items.title: Saudi Aramco chief warns of 'scarily thin’ global oil stockpiles, amid war on Iran
items.summary: Saudi Aramco chief warns of 'scarily thin’ global oil stockpiles, amid war on Iran The chief executive of Saudi Aramco warned that the world's oil stockpiles are now "scarily thin". In his first public speech since the US-Israel war on Iran began, Amin Nasser said the conflict reduced oil supply from the region by "nearly 3bn barrels", with over 1bn barrels of oil released from reserves to cushion the depletion. Nasser estimated that "less than 6bn barrels of commercial inventories remain today, with the vast majority not practically available". "The system is already straining," he told the Energy Intelligence Forum conference in London. "And with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin."

clusters.headline: Hormuz Strait disruptions could lead to global food security crisis

items.title: Hormuz Strait disruptions could lead to global food security crisis
items.summary: Hormuz Strait disruptions could lead to global food security crisis Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz could lead to a global food security crisis, the secretary general of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), John Denton, warned. According to the Wall Street Journal, Denton indicated that if the vital waterway is not reopened, grain prices could rise by up to 80 percent. The situation in the strait has also caused a shortage of around 2.7 million tons of fertiliser on the world market, a decrease of nearly 40 percent. Such obstacles could affect international agricultural production and food supplies, making import-dependent countries especially vulnerable. The report noted that the ICC is working with the UN and the International Maritime Organization on a mechanism that would transfer temporary management of navigation through the waterway to the UN secretary general. However, the ongoing tensions between the US and Iran have hindered its implementation, the report added.

clusters.headline: Despite war US military is leaving a stronger Iraq behind

items.title: Despite war US military is leaving a stronger Iraq behind
items.summary: On September 30, the U.S. completed the withdrawal of its troops from Iraq. Heralding this event, Iraq declared “Sovereignty Day,” celebrating the end of U.S. occupation and return of full sovereignty to the people of Iraq. In practice, this withdrawal was little more than the departure of a few hundred soldiers that had returned to Iraq in 2014 – at the invitation of the Iraqi government – to provide support and assistance to the collapsing Iraqi Army in its fight against ISIS. Unlike the hundreds of thousands of troops needed in Germany and Japan at the end of WWII, the troops of Operation Inherent Resolve were neither an occupation nor a challenge to sovereign control. Nonetheless, the mission had become a political liability and a convenient excuse for anti-government militias to maintain independence, retain weapons and force its will both in the streets and within Parliament. While some voices in Washington argue for a keeping residual military presence , the reasonable solution is shifting to a diplomatic and development effort. clusters.headline: CIA report warns of civil conflict and 'collapse' in Israel: Report

items.title: CIA report warns of civil conflict and 'collapse' in Israel: Report
items.summary: CIA report warns of civil conflict and 'collapse' in Israel: Report Israel is at risk of internal collapse or civil war because of tensions among Israelis, an August report by CIA experts tasked with providing “alternative analysis” said, according to a report by Drop Site News published on Monday. The CIA report, titled “Fracture From Within", said that Israel faces a volatile situation ahead of 27 October elections, where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will be fighting for his political future. items.title: The case for pulling US military back from the first island chain
items.summary: Late last month, Japan’s defense ministry made an unsettling announcement. A U.S. ground-based missile system, known as the Typhon and capable of firing Tomahawk missiles, would not return to the United States after being deployed to Japan for military exercises. Instead, it would be stored at Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, at least temporarily. Tokyo tried to downplay the move, noting that the decision was intended to support training, not warfighting, and that no U.S. Army units would deploy with the missile system. But the reassuring language is unlikely to forestall the negative consequences of the posture change: an increase in military tensions along the first island chain in East Asia. The timing of the decision, following closely on the heels of the visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington , may seem out of sync with Donald Trump’s “dovish” outreach to Beijing. But the contradiction is a feature, not a bug, of the Trump administration’s Asia policy. clusters.headline: Can Kurds in Iraq unite as US troops withdraw from the country?

items.title: Can Kurds in Iraq unite as US troops withdraw from the country?
items.summary: On September 21, the Kurdistan Region of Iraq officially announced the completion of the long-delayed unification and reorganization of its Peshmerga paramilitary forces under the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs (MoPA). The Peshmerga are Kurdish armed forces, with roots going back to Kurdish guerrillas who fought as a more or less united front against successive Iraqi governments for most of the 20th century. After the 2003 invasion, though, they never came together as one Kurdish national army. Instead, they split into two separate party forces, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), each tied to one of the region's dominant political factions. Kurdish leaders hailed the September unification announcement as a historic victory for the Kurds in Iraq. Notably, the unification happened nine days before the final U.S. military withdrawal from Iraq. The timing raises an important question: as Washington shrinks its direct military presence in Iraq, what security architecture will it leave behind? Zardari called for differences to be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, emphasising the importance of safe maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, according to a statement from his office. items.title: Attacks on Hormuz shipping at wartime high, report says
items.summary: Attacks on Hormuz shipping at wartime high, report says Iranian missile and drone attacks on ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz were at their most intense in the two weeks to 11 October, the highest level since the US-Israeli strikes began seven months ago, the Financial Times reported. The next most intense period of attacks was during the first two weeks of March, when 13 ships were hit, the newspaper said, citing data from naval agency UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which monitors marine security in the region. Shipowners are reconsider carrying cargoes in the region, the report said. Six vessels were attacked on Sunday alone, making it the deadliest day of attacks on shipping near the strait since the start of the conflict, FT calculated. It added that oil shipments through Hormuz fell to just 2.9 million barrels on 11 October, the lowest daily volume this month, according to Kpler.

items.title: 'Major wipeout' of 2006 proportions could force a new GOP reckoning
items.summary: Republicans could be looking at a major wipeout in the midterm elections. Their tiny House majority was always going to be difficult to maintain, but the Senate should not be in play at all. Yet it surely is, with Democrats leading in nearly all the toss-up races , including in the reddest states, and competitive in at least a dozen of the contests that will determine which party controls the upper chamber. The Iran war is a big reason this has come to pass. It has demoralized the least indefatigably partisan part of President Donald Trump’s coalition by abandoning his promise to avoid new forever wars in the Middle East. His sharpest critics see this as ranging from sycophantic revenge on the general officer class to simply misguided personnel policy. items.title: Why Saudi Arabia has returned to war in Yemen
items.summary: This article was republished with permission from the Arab Center Washington DC. When Ansar Allah—commonly referred to as the Houthis— seized Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandab Strait on September 10, 2026, they appeared to gain the upper hand in Yemen’s long-running conflict. However, in early October Saudi-backed government forces began to retake some of the captured territory and Saudi Arabia launched a punishing assault on Houthi positions from the air. France , Pakistan , and the United States have all sent personnel to help the kingdom counter the Houthi offensive. Outside the region, some have portrayed the Houthi offensive as another theater within the broader US-Israeli war on Iran. However, this broader regional war is separate from the war in Yemen, which can be traced back to the Houthi takeover of Yemen’s capital Sanaa in September 2014 and the decision by neighboring Saudi Arabia to launch a coalition to oust them in March 2015. "On Oct 11, tanker MT PETRO DOLPHIN, carrying 11 Indian seafarers, was subjected to a drone attack at Sohar Anchorage," Indian Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said in a post on X. "While nine of our Indian crew members have been successfully rescued and are safe, two Indian nationals currently remain missing." Sonowal added that India is "continuously coordinating with all relevant authorities to fully support the ongoing rescue efforts and ensure every possible action is taken to safely locate our missing personnel". Since the war on Iran began in late February, at least 16 Indian seafarers have been killed.

items.title: Iran’s security chief calls US response to deal conditions ‘inadequate’
items.summary: Iran’s security chief calls US response to deal conditions ‘inadequate’ Washington must clarify its position before talks on a possible agreement can advance, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei says. “The Americans have now responded to us. In their response, they have accepted some of our conditions, while others remain unclear,” the Supreme National Security Council secretary told the semi-official Tasnim news agency. Rezaei described the US response as “inadequate”. “We are no longer in the process of responding to the Americans,” he said. “They must clarify the issues that remain unclear to us,” he added. The exchange follows President Donald Trump’s rejection late last month of an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. US Vice President JD Vance subsequently demanded a “meaningful” reduction in Iran’s uranium enrichment capacity as a condition for an agreement.

Iran’s Supreme National Security Council secretary said the UAE military and the commander of US Central Command also participate in the operation, according to state-linked news agency ISNA. Trump “claims every day that the Strait of Hormuz is open, but in response I say: ‘You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iranian control and we manage it,'” Rezaei said. items.title: Houthis claim responsibility for deadly Riyadh airport attack
items.summary: Houthis claim responsibility for deadly Riyadh airport attack Yemen’s Houthis say they carried out Saturday’s missile attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid Airport, which killed 12 people and wounded about 300, some critically. Military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched several operations against the airport, “resulting in the disruption of air traffic at the airport and its complete closure”. He also named King Fahd Airport in Dammam, an Aramco-affiliated petrol station and a refinery in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Region as targets. The Riyadh strike caused the highest death toll from an attack on a Gulf country since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on 28 February. King Khalid Airport remained closed on Sunday.

EU warned that strikes by "Iran’s proxies" risk pushing the region into a wider cycle of violence. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the attack as a “dangerous escalation” and called on the Houthis to stop targeting civilian infrastructure. “These attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwaves sent through the world. These murderous attacks on civilians must stop at once,” the EU chief wrote on X on Sunday. She added that the EU stood in “solidarity with Saudi Arabia”. items.title: Iranian nuclear technology safe from US attacks, says atomic energy chief
items.summary: Iranian nuclear technology safe from US attacks, says atomic energy chief The head of Iran's atomic energy agency said on Sunday that the country's nuclear technology is safe from external disruption and cannot be halted by threats, pressure or attacks. Mohammad Eslami, the chief of the Atomic Energy Organisation of Iran (AEOI), said Iran's nuclear advances are a national achievement and were a testament to the dedication of Iranian scientists. “Overt threats by US officials to use tactical weapons against Iran’s nuclear facilities - delivered right from the United Nations podium - and talk of destroying Iran’s ancient civilisation, reveal helplessness in the face of a pioneering nation that has historically been the cradle of science, knowledge and technology,” Eslami was quoted as saying by Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency, adding that the nation will not surrender to excessive demands. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly affirmed Washington's intention to wipe out Iran's nuclear capabilities and ensure that the country will never be able to develop the technology.

"Ik zag met mijn eigen ogen de gewonden. Iedereen rende weg." items.title: Trump says Iran is ‘failing badly’ as conflict in Yemen widens
items.summary: Trump says Iran is ‘failing badly’ as conflict in Yemen widens US President Donald Trump on Friday left open the possibility of further military action against Iran as fighting intensifies in Yemen and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have led to a renewed offensive. Asked why possible US military action against Iran might be delayed until after the 3 November midterm elections rather than carried out immediately, Trump told reporters: “Well, we may. I think we’ll see, but I think that, uh, they’re failing badly. Their country is failing badly." "The military is defeated. They have no navy, they have no air force. Uh, they have 300 percent inflation and, uh, Iran is in very bad shape.” The remarks, recorded in a transcript of Trump’s 9 October press briefing, did not include a specific timeline or details of what action Washington might take. The US and Israel launched their war against Iran on 28 February. Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region, while disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has threatened global energy supplies. Read more: Trump

items.summary: Israeli politician says assassinating Ali Khamenei was a ‘mistake’ The leader of Israel’s Democrats party on Saturday has called the assassination of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei a “mistake”. “I think, unequivocally, the elimination of Khamenei, the father, was a mistake - not because he didn’t deserve to die, only because it doesn’t serve the interests of the State of Israel,” Yair Golan said. He also added that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s goal of toppling the Iranian government was “unrealistic”. Khamenei was assassinated at the beginning of the US-Israel war and has been succeeded by his son, Mojtaba. The new supreme leader is believed to be far less risk-averse than his father, who had issued a fatwa in 2003 banning nuclear weapons in Iran. items.title: Increased vessel attacks drive Hormuz oil exports 'sharply lower', report says
items.summary: Increased vessel attacks drive Hormuz oil exports 'sharply lower', report says Hormuz oil exports were “sharply lower,” falling to a seven-day average of 9.9 million barrels per day as of October 7, 42 percent below prewar levels and down from about 15.5 million in September, according to Kpler data cited by the Financial Times. Kpler said that flows had recovered to prewar levels in September but "intensified attacks on vessels" had driven exports "sharply lower" this week. Energy analyst Rory Johnston also said that the latest estimate puts Hormuz seven-day average oil flow peaking at 16.2 mbpd on September 24. "Then Iran really picked up its shipping attacks and that flow unsurprisingly pulled back by 3-4 mbpd," he wrote on X. "Now seeing flow at 12-13 mbpd over the past two weeks."

Speaking to NourNews agency, Boroujerdi said that Iran's nuclear programme is pursued  according to the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. Earlier, Vance said that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the war. "If you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel. items.title: 2027: The Ukraine winter we prayed wouldn't come
items.summary: Let’s imagine a bit of “future history” in Ukraine. It is February 2027. The Ukrainian winter has been unusually cold, and Russian air strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, transportation grid, and communications networks have been increasingly destructive. Ukraine has no effective defenses against massive barrages of Russian missiles, glide bombs, and jet-powered drones, as Russian President Vladimir Putin seeks both to cripple Ukraine’s ability to field an effective military and to break its will to continue fighting. Lacking heat, water, and electricity, millions of Ukrainians are fleeing Kyiv and other major cities. Western embassies are temporarily relocating from the capital to safer environs. Russian attacks on data centers and Starlink terminals begin to erode Ukraine’s battlefield targeting and communications, jeopardizing its prospects for holding the last two “fortress cities” in the Donbas region once warmer weather allows ground combat to intensify. items.summary: The Bunker appears originally at the Project on Government Oversight and is republished here with permission. The U.S. ended its military campaign in Iraq on September 30, as the final American combat troops based there left the country. Their departure ended 23 years of fitful fighting. They found no weapons of mass destruction , which was the battering ram President George W. Bush and his combative coterie used to scaremonger the U.S to invade in 2003. The first time the window-rattling roar of a B-1 bomber woke me up this summer, I thought for one crazed second we were under attack. By the second time, I’d learned to recognise the sound of US planes taking off from their base at RAF Fairford for what it was: a reminder that although Britain wants no part in this war with Iran, we cannot quite escape the consequences. We’ll feel them at the petrol pump , or in the supermarket this autumn, or in this winter’s heating bills . But living under the flight path adds an extra edge to it. The skies finally fell silent last week, but only because the bombers have been hastily summoned home after an alleged terrorist plot to attack Fairford, in which (according to the prime minister) there are “ strong indications that Iran played a part ”. items.title: Is Iran poised to withdraw from the Non-Proliferation Treaty?
items.summary: In September, as the media focused its attention on the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz and the debates at the U.N. General Assembly, some internal developments in Iran went all but unnoticed. On September 28, 32 Iranian conservatives published an open letter calling for Iran to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) as a matter of urgency. Since the “ snapback ” of U.N. sanctions on Iran in September 2025, ultraconservative Iranian lawmakers have regularly pushed for pulling out of the NPT, under which the vast majority of states have committed to not develop nuclear weapons. The Majles — Iran’s parliament — drafted a law that would have initiated the move in 2025, but it has yet to move forward. In September, some lawmakers submitted new “triple-urgency” legislation to the Majles ’ president, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, who is also currently Iran’s chief negotiator These continuous calls by ultraconservatives to withdraw from the NPT have yet to produce an actual withdrawal because of a lack of political consensus. items.title: Will Americans ever escape this 'imperialist realism'?
items.summary: Last week, after nearly two decades of fighting, the U.S. finally pulled the plug on its seemingly endless war in Iraq. Like our exit from Afghanistan just a few years ago, the end of fighting in Iraq was met with an eerie quiet. It doesn’t take much to figure out why so little attention is paid to the end of these wars: they mark yet another loss for America and the people in Washington who insist our military power can solve every problem, everywhere. Both conflicts are examples of American hubris — strategically incoherent wars fought with American lives at the expense of too many Iraqis and Afghans lives. But, of course, we refuse to learn our lesson. The week before Americans finally vacated Iraq, President Donald Trump took to his proverbial pulpit at the U.N. to brag about his exploitation of Venezuela for oil, declaring “to the victor goes the spoils.” It was a stark expression of how America’s domination of the global order — it’s imperialism, if you will — really works. items.title: Saudi Arabia says three dead at airports after Houthis claim attacks
items.summary: Saudi Arabia says three dead at airports after Houthis claim attacks Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people were killed in attacks on two of the kingdom's international airports, including in the capital, Riyadh, after Yemen's Houthis claimed to have fired on both transport hubs. The Iran-aligned Houthis took responsibility earlier for a flurry of attacks that included firing a ballistic missile at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, as the conflict deepens with Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government. "On Tuesday and Wednesday... Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport were subjected to attacks targeting their facilities," the kingdom's civil aviation authority said in a statement, without blaming anyone for the attacks. An Egyptian and an Algerian national were killed at Abha airport, and a Sudanese national was killed at the airport in Riyadh, the agency said, with 36 people wounded in the attacks.

items.title: The Guardian view on the US midterms: the cost of living is on the ballot, but this is about democracy too | Editorial
items.summary: Donald Trump’s unpopularity and the economic struggles of voters have boosted Democrats. But with less than a month to go, there is no complacency For once, Democrats and Donald Trump might be in agreement: “Pretend I’m on the ticket,” the historically unpopular president has instructed supporters . Midterms are in large part a referendum on the incumbent, and Trump’s war on Iran and its impact on the cost of living have boosted support for Democrats. With less than a month to go, they have reason to be upbeat . The party has a mountain to climb after the devastating defeats of 2024, and the gerrymandering of Republicans, but surveys give it a lead of about nine points on the generic ballot, which measures preference for parties rather than specific candidates. Attention has turned from the prospects of seizing the House, where Democrats are forecast a clear majority, to what once seemed like the highly optimistic possibility of taking the Senate too. items.title: Blockers by Michael Lewis review – the quiet heroes who tried to stop Doge
items.summary: The author of Moneyball brings his exceptional narrative skills to bear on Musk’s anti-government crusade Donald Trump’s catastrophic errors get so much attention that his systemic ones can easily be missed. While the world looks on in dismay at his farcical war in Iran, the thuggery of Ice agents or clownish attacks on erstwhile allies like Canada and Denmark, the core functions of the American government are slowly disintegrating. It is harder to get people to focus on the machinery of the state because the effects are often slow and hard to pin down. Outbreaks of disease – such as the recent wave of explosive diarrhoea across the US – might have happened anyway, but were probably made worse by lay-offs at the Centers for Disease Control. Likewise, Trump is not directly responsible for natural disasters, but response times in the past year may have been hampered by mass redundancies at the National Weather Service. Cuts to tax collection also seem to have reduced revenue by multiple billions, though we cannot be sure of the causal relationship. Continue reading...

items.title: Vance says Iran must cut nuclear enrichment capacity to reach deal with US
items.summary: Vance says Iran must cut nuclear enrichment capacity to reach deal with US US Vice President JD Vance said that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the war. "If you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel. That's a very basic threshold issue," Vance said during an interview with Reuters. "I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity." Vance also indicated that the US remained open to an agreement but would require concrete Iranian nuclear concessions. "We're not going to trade words for actions," he said.

items.summary: California leaders condemn Trump’s remarks about possible attacks on US cities California political leaders on Tuesday condemned President Donald Trump after he said Iran could “take out” US cities including Los Angeles and San Diego, describing the remarks as dangerous and unacceptable. Speaking at a political rally on Monday, Trump was discussing the economic costs of war when he said: “It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let ’em take out Los Angeles, let ’em take out San Diego.” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said Trump’s remarks could compromise the city’s safety, while San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria said: “We are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.” California Governor Gavin Newsom also criticised Trump, calling him “deranged”. Republican congressional candidate Jim Desmond said he “vehemently” disagreed with the president, adding that “no American city is expendable and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”

items.summary: US and several allies say Iran committed 'terrorist actions' The US and nine other countries across the Americas in a joint statement condemned what they called Iran's "terrorist actions". The joint statement was released by the US and endorsed by Argentina, Canada, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Guyana, Paraguay, Peru, and Trinidad and Tobago. "On 5 October, the undersigned nations, condemn the terrorist actions and other malign influence operations in our hemisphere by Iran and its terrorist proxies," it read. "These hostile efforts include a range of Iranian and proxy-sponsored lethal plotting, illicit fundraising, political interference and foreign influence activities, and operations meant to bolster terrorist networks, coerce perceived enemies, compromise legal or administrative processes, and harm regional security." The joint statement indicated that the countries "stand united" against "such threats", demanding that Tehran and "its proxies must halt these actions now".

items.title: Saudi Aramco chief warns of 'scarily thin’ global oil stockpiles, amid war on Iran
items.summary: Saudi Aramco chief warns of 'scarily thin’ global oil stockpiles, amid war on Iran The chief executive of Saudi Aramco warned that the world's oil stockpiles are now "scarily thin". In his first public speech since the US-Israel war on Iran began, Amin Nasser said the conflict reduced oil supply from the region by "nearly 3bn barrels", with over 1bn barrels of oil released from reserves to cushion the depletion. Nasser estimated that "less than 6bn barrels of commercial inventories remain today, with the vast majority not practically available". "The system is already straining," he told the Energy Intelligence Forum conference in London. "And with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin."

items.title: Hormuz Strait disruptions could lead to global food security crisis
items.summary: Hormuz Strait disruptions could lead to global food security crisis Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz could lead to a global food security crisis, the secretary general of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), John Denton, warned. According to the Wall Street Journal, Denton indicated that if the vital waterway is not reopened, grain prices could rise by up to 80 percent. The situation in the strait has also caused a shortage of around 2.7 million tons of fertiliser on the world market, a decrease of nearly 40 percent. Such obstacles could affect international agricultural production and food supplies, making import-dependent countries especially vulnerable. The report noted that the ICC is working with the UN and the International Maritime Organization on a mechanism that would transfer temporary management of navigation through the waterway to the UN secretary general. However, the ongoing tensions between the US and Iran have hindered its implementation, the report added.

items.title: Despite war US military is leaving a stronger Iraq behind
items.summary: On September 30, the U.S. completed the withdrawal of its troops from Iraq. Heralding this event, Iraq declared “Sovereignty Day,” celebrating the end of U.S. occupation and return of full sovereignty to the people of Iraq. In practice, this withdrawal was little more than the departure of a few hundred soldiers that had returned to Iraq in 2014 – at the invitation of the Iraqi government – to provide support and assistance to the collapsing Iraqi Army in its fight against ISIS. Unlike the hundreds of thousands of troops needed in Germany and Japan at the end of WWII, the troops of Operation Inherent Resolve were neither an occupation nor a challenge to sovereign control. Nonetheless, the mission had become a political liability and a convenient excuse for anti-government militias to maintain independence, retain weapons and force its will both in the streets and within Parliament. While some voices in Washington argue for a keeping residual military presence , the reasonable solution is shifting to a diplomatic and development effort. items.summary: Houthis target Riyadh airpot, declare Saudi airspace open target except for holy sites The Iran-affiliated Yemeni group targeted King Khaled International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh for the second time on Monday. "In response to the Saudi aggression against our country in the past 24 hours ... the Yemeni armed forces targeted King Khaled Airport in Riyadh," the military spokesperson said in a statement. The statement said the strike was precise and disrupted air traffic at the airport. The strike comes after the Houthis issued an earlier warning on Monday against using Saudi airspace. "The Saudi skies are open theatre for our operations, except for the holy airspaces of Makkah and Madinah," the Houthi warning said. "We disclaim all liability for the consequences of ignoring our warnings against continuing to use the Saudi airspace," it added.

Instead, it would be stored at Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, at least temporarily. items.title: Can Kurds in Iraq unite as US troops withdraw from the country?
items.summary: On September 21, the Kurdistan Region of Iraq officially announced the completion of the long-delayed unification and reorganization of its Peshmerga paramilitary forces under the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs (MoPA). The Peshmerga are Kurdish armed forces, with roots going back to Kurdish guerrillas who fought as a more or less united front against successive Iraqi governments for most of the 20th century. After the 2003 invasion, though, they never came together as one Kurdish national army. Instead, they split into two separate party forces, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), each tied to one of the region's dominant political factions. Kurdish leaders hailed the September unification announcement as a historic victory for the Kurds in Iraq. Notably, the unification happened nine days before the final U.S. military withdrawal from Iraq. The timing raises an important question: as Washington shrinks its direct military presence in Iraq, what security architecture will it leave behind? A campaign of heavy bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war launched by the US and Israel in late February, and Washington in recent weeks has dialled back military operations in favor of economic pressure. items.summary: Iran's diplomat said on Sunday there was no military solution to the US war against Iran as peace talks appeared stalled.
